brewing.notes: A common starting point for herbal infusions: boiling water, about five minutes.

description:
An insect tea from around Sidonggou in Chishui, Guizhou: the tiny droppings of moth larvae fed on fermented leaves are collected and dried. Output is reported at only a little over 200 jin.

Brew it as you would other herbal infusions. If the plant is new to you, check that it is safe for you first, especially when pregnant or on medication.
history: It is reported to have been a tribute tea in the Qing dynasty, and local accounts say it is still served at state guesthouses. Traditionally the larvae fed on Platycarya leaves, which explains its other local name. Little more is documented.
processing: Young leaves from old white tea trees are fermented to attract a moth whose larvae eat them; their droppings are gathered and sun-dried.
harvest_season: Depends on the plant and the place.
appearance_liquor: Depends on the plant; usually pale to amber.
taste_profile: A herbal infusion; the taste depends on the plant.
vintage_note: Herbal infusions are not sold by vintage: buy recent stock and use it within a year or so.
